Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
This is a much stronger study than the pilot: randomised, pre-registered, with administrative output and timesheet hours. It already avoids most of the problems I raised there. **The arithmetic checks out, and the main conclusions are largely supported.** The remaining issues concern inference with few clusters, outcomes reported without a control comparison, hidden costs, and how the per-hour result is interpreted.

## Arithmetic check

Everything I recomputed is consistent:

- **Hours.** 33.0 / 37.9 is −12.9%, and 31.2 / 37.6 is −17.0%. The scheduled cut from 37.5 to 30 is −20%.
- **Output per actual hour.** Case-processing: 0.979 / 0.871 = +12.5%. Counter: 0.886 / 0.830 = +6.7%. Both match the table.
- **Scheduled-hours comparison.** 0.979 / 0.8 = +22%, as stated. The paper doesn't give the counter equivalent: 0.886 / 0.8 = +10.75%. That's worth adding, because it shows the scheduled-hours overstatement in both strata.

## 1. Clustered standard errors with 10–14 clusters

The counter stratum has 10 clusters (5 v 5) and case-processing has 14. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are biased downward with this few clusters, so the CIs are probably too narrow.

The tight counter interval (−16.9 to −5.9 from 10 offices) and the per-hour interval that barely excludes zero (+0.4 to +13.3) are most at risk. Randomisation inference, or a wild cluster bootstrap with small-sample corrections, would be the standard fix. Since randomisation was within strata, randomisation inference is natural here. Was a small-cluster correction in the registered plan?

## 2. Several results in Table 1 aren't difference-in-differences estimates

The table is titled "Difference-in-differences estimates," but:

- **Waiting time** (4.2 → 6.9 minutes) is a pre/post change in treated offices only, with no control comparison. Waiting time is a registered secondary outcome, so it should get the same DiD treatment and a CI.
- **Abandoned calls** (6% → 10%) appear only in the text and are treated-only as well.
- **Quality** (3.1% v 3.0%; 11.8% v 10.9%) looks like a month-9 cross-sectional comparison, without a pre-period or CI.
- **Sick days and resignations** have no CIs.

The counter repeat-contact rate rose from 10.9% to 11.8%, about 8% in relative terms, and the text doesn't discuss it. It belongs alongside the waiting-time and abandonment results as a sign of worse service.

## 3. Registered primary analysis and the heterogeneity claim

The Summary leads with "the effect differed sharply by type of work," but the paper doesn't say whether the registered primary analysis was:

- a pooled estimate, or
- stratum-specific estimates with a pre-specified interaction test.

If a pooled estimate was registered, it should be reported first. Either way, the stratum difference needs a formal interaction test. The two CIs overlap slightly (−6.8 vs −5.9), so the difference isn't self-evidently significant, especially after a small-cluster correction.

Also, strata were not randomised, so the contrast between them is not itself an experimental estimate. Presence-dependence is a plausible explanation, but office size, management and caseload may also differ between strata. The Discussion's generalisation ("what matters is whether output... depends on hours of presence") is a reasonable hypothesis, not an experimental finding.

## 4. Case-processing: hidden costs and unreported backlog

- **Overtime cost.** Treated case-processing staff worked about 33 actual hours against a 30-hour schedule, with overtime "claimed." That means full 37.5-hour pay plus roughly 3 hours a week of overtime, possibly at a premium, for output about 2% lower. Labour cost per case closed probably rose by around 10% or more. The county's question was whether this could be done "without loss of service." Service held up in case-processing, but at higher cost, and the paper doesn't report it.
- **Backlog is measurable now.** The Limitations defer backlog growth to the 24-month follow-up. But queue length, time to decision, and the share of cases within statutory deadlines are all in the case-management system. Cases closed can be held up by prioritising simpler cases, so these measures matter now.
- **The overturn rate is right-censored.** Appeals on decisions made in months 7–9 may not have been resolved by the analysis date. An unchanged overturn rate at nine months is weaker reassurance than it looks.
- **The CI includes a moderate loss.** "Little or no measurable loss" is fair as a description of the point estimate. However, the CI includes losses up to 6.8%, so the paper should say a moderate loss is not ruled out.

## 5. Counter offices: the per-hour gain is mostly utilisation

"Each hour worked was somewhat more productive" is probably the wrong interpretation. With fewer staff present during unchanged opening hours, queues lengthen and each staff-hour has less idle time between contacts. Output per hour rises mechanically through higher utilisation, and the public pays for it in waiting time and abandoned calls.

That is queueing arithmetic, not evidence that rested staff work faster. The paper's point that per-hour and per-employee productivity diverge is correct. It should go further and say that in coverage-bound work, the per-hour gain is largely a cost shifted to the public.

Relatedly, this result depends on the chosen implementation: unchanged opening hours with no extra staff. That's a legitimate design, but the conclusion should be framed as "without additional staffing" rather than as a property of the work type.

## 6. Possible spillover between offices

- **Case-processing.** If case queues are shared county-wide (e.g., permits routed across offices), work could shift between treated and control offices.
- **Counter and phone.** If counters serve overlapping areas, or phone lines route calls county-wide, longer waits in treated offices may push contacts to control offices. That would inflate control output and overstate the negative effect.

The design section should say whether queues and call routing are office-specific.

## 7. Sick days: exposure and schedule format

The DiD design handles seasonality, unlike the pilot, but not exposure. If the 30 hours were delivered as fewer days, staff had fewer scheduled days on which to be absent, and sick days per FTE fall mechanically. The paper doesn't state the schedule format. Sick days per scheduled day, or sickness hours as a share of scheduled hours, would settle this.

## 8. The meetings analysis

The caveats are appropriately strong, and registering a confirmatory test is good practice. Three additions would help:

- **The correlation is very imprecise.** With r = 0.71 and n = 7, the 95% CI is roughly −0.09 to 0.95, so it includes zero. Stating this would reinforce the caveat.
- **There is no baseline.** Meeting time was measured only in month six, so the 3.3-hour gap could partly predate the trial. Pre-period calendar data, if retrievable, would fix this.
- **The paper's own numbers support the hypothesis.** Subtracting meeting time from actual hours gives:
  - treated non-meeting time: 33.0 − 3.8 = 29.2 hours;
  - control non-meeting time: 37.9 − 7.1 = 30.8 hours.

  That is only about 5% less non-meeting time. With output down 2.1%, output per non-meeting hour rises by only about 3%, compared with 12.5% per actual hour. Most of the per-hour gain would then be explained by removed meeting time rather than more productive work. This is still exploratory, since it assumes meetings produce no measured output. It is, however, a sharper statement of the hypothesis for the 24-month confirmatory test.

## Smaller points

- Show pre-period trends by arm, since the DiD relies on parallel trends over the six-month pre-period.
- Define FTE for treated staff: whether a 30-hour employee at full pay still counts as 1.0 FTE.
- Report the extent of overtime in control offices, so the treated overtime can be interpreted as a difference.

## Overall

This trial is well designed and appropriately cautious, and it directly corrects the main failure of the uncontrolled pilot: computing per-hour gains against scheduled hours. Fixing the small-cluster inference, making all secondary outcomes DiD with CIs, and reporting overtime cost and backlog would leave its conclusions on solid ground. The counter-office per-hour finding should be reframed as utilisation rather than productivity.
